passages.t: ‘Clap your hands, all you peoples’: God is King of all the earth
passages.happening:
This short psalm is loud. “Clap your hands, all you peoples; shout unto God with a voice of triumph” (verse 1). The reason follows. “How awesome is the LORD Most High, the great King over all the earth!” (verse 2).

Israel remembers what God did for them. He gave them their land, “the pride of Jacob, whom He loves” (verse 4).

Then a scene. “God has ascended amid shouts of joy, the LORD with the sound of the horn” (verse 5). The call to praise comes four times in one verse: “Sing praises to God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises!” (verse 6).

The end is wide. “God reigns over the nations; God is seated on His holy throne” (verse 8). “The nobles of the nations have assembled as the people of the God of Abraham” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Clapping and shouting were the sounds of a coronation. When the boy Joash was made king, “the people clapped their hands and declared, ‘Long live the king!’” (2 Kings 11:12). So the psalm sounds like a crowning, with God as the King.

The horn is the shofar, a ram's horn. It was blown to gather people, to sound alarm and to mark holy days.

‘Ascended’ most likely pictures God going up to his throne. Many think this was acted out when the ark of the covenant, the gold chest that stood for God's throne on earth, was carried up to the temple on Zion with music. When David first brought the ark to Jerusalem, it came “with shouting and the sounding of the ram’s horn” (2 Samuel 6:15). Some scholars think there was a yearly feast that celebrated God as King. The Old Testament does not describe one directly, so this remains a view.

The ‘shields of the earth’ (verse 9) are the rulers who protect their peoples. They too belong to God.
passages.later:
Verse 9 sees the nations gathered ‘as the people of the God of Abraham’. God had promised Abraham, “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). Paul says that people from every nation who trust Christ are counted in: “And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:29).

Many Christians also read verse 5 of Jesus going up into heaven: “they watched as He was taken up, and a cloud hid Him from their sight” (Acts 1:9).
passages.asks:
Verse 3 says God “subdues nations beneath us”. Read on, and verse 9 has the nations gathered in as God's own people. The psalm's hope is not that one people wins and others lose. It is that all of them end up praising the same King.

This psalm asks for noise. Not every prayer is quiet. When did you last praise God out loud, with others, for being King of all the earth?
